Bresnahan, MD Anderson Cancer Center (Bhattacharya Lab) 2026-10-30 Home placenta-xqtl-federated lets cohorts with placental RNA-seq and genotype data take part in a multi-ancestry placental xQTL study without sharing individual-level data. Each cohort runs the pipeline on its own computers and sends only summary-level files (A–J) to MD Anderson Cancer Center (MDACC), which combines them across cohorts and ancestry groups. Pipeline version: 1.0.0-dev. These pages are built from the docs/ folder of the repository; the same pages are included inside the pipeline image for offline reading. Where to start Cohort investigators: read the Collaboration brief for the aims, the analyses each site runs and the files requested. Analysts running the pipeline: start with the quick start below, then the HPC configuration guide. Results: the appendix Seadragon validation shows what the site smoke test checks on a real cluster. Quick start The pipeline is distributed as one self-contained image (software, public reference data, Java and Nextflow). It needs no internet access at the site. apptainer pull xqtl-federated_<version>.sif oras://ghcr.io/sbresnahan/xqtl-federated-sif:<version> sha256sum -c xqtl-federated_<version>.sif.sha256 apptainer run xqtl-federated_<version>.sif bootstrap ./xqtl ./xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile seadragon,smoke ./xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile seadragon -params-file cohort.yml --mode prepare_references ./xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile seadragon -params-file cohort.yml --mode site Replace seadragon with your scheduler and engine, for example -profile slurm,apptainer -c mysite.config (see Executors). The restricted file Site runs need xqtl-restricted-<version>.tar.gz, a small file that holds the shared splicing clusters and the MDACC signal list. MDACC sends it by email after the data-sharing agreement is approved. If your site has not received it, request it from the scientific contact, Sean T. Bresnahan (stbresnahan@mdanderson.org), stating your cohort, the pipeline version and the approved agreement. Do not redistribute it. Licence The pipeline is GPL-3.0. Collaboration brief Collaboration brief: proposed analyses and summary files requested from participating cohorts Project: Multi-ancestry placental xQTL atlas Prepared for: Participating placental cohort investigators, including PACEplacenta collaborators Coordinating institution: MD Anderson Cancer Center (MDACC), Bhattacharya Lab Scientific contact: Sean T. Bresnahan (stbresnahan@mdanderson.org) Analysis software: MDACC-provided self-contained pipeline (first release in preparation) 1. Purpose of the collaboration We are studying how fetal genetic differences affect RNA produced by the placenta and whether conditions during pregnancy, such as maternal glucose levels or BMI, change those effects. We will combine results from cohorts with different genetic ancestries to identify placental genes and RNA forms that may be relevant to birth outcomes and childhood metabolic health. \[1, 2\] For cohorts that cannot transfer participant-level data to MDACC, each cohort runs the analyses on its own computing system. It reviews the summary files and sends MDACC only those approved under its data-sharing rules. No participant-level genotypes, RNA-seq files, molecular measurements, or clinical records are sent to MDACC. Separately, each site must upload quality-controlled genotype files to the external TOPMed Imputation Server, as described in Section 5. Cohorts able to share de-identified individual-level data may discuss a separate arrangement with MDACC under an appropriate agreement. This document describes the planned analyses, what each cohort would run locally, what MDACC would do with the shared results, and which files sites would send. The final section lists possible later analyses that would require discussion with collaborators before any additional work or data sharing. 2. Research questions and planned analyses 2.1 Identify genetic effects on different RNA measurements We aim to identify genetic variants that affect placental RNA measurements, including changes that gene-level expression alone may miss. Using a placenta-specific reference built from long-read RNA sequencing (HPLRv2), participating sites will measure nine types of RNA features: gene expression, isoform expression, isoform usage, splicing, intron retention, alternative transcription start sites, alternative polyadenylation, RNA editing, and RNA stability. For each RNA feature, sites will test which nearby fetal genetic variants are associated with its measurement (cis-xQTL analysis), separately for each eligible ancestry group. The analyses will also identify independent genetic signals within each region. \[3, 4\] Sites will estimate the proportions of major placental cell types using a public single-cell RNA reference. These estimates will be included in the statistical models to account for differences among samples. At significant xQTL signals from the site’s own analysis, and at a list of xQTL signals supplied by MDACC, sites will also test whether the genetic association changes with the proportion of a cell type, such as trophoblast, endothelial, or stromal cells. \[5\] MDACC will combine association results across cohorts and ancestry groups to identify consistent and varying genetic effects. We will also use each cohort’s linkage disequilibrium (LD) results, which describe correlations among nearby genetic variants, to narrow the list of candidate causal variants across ancestries. \[6\] 2.2 Compare placental findings with birth and childhood health studies We will integrate placental xQTL results with publicly available genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics for birth weight, gestational duration, childhood BMI and anthropometric traits, glycemic phenotypes, and youth-onset type 2 diabetes. Planned analyses include statistical fine-mapping, colocalization to assess whether placental xQTL and GWAS signals may share causal variants, and transcriptome-wide association analyses (TWAS), which use genetic evidence to prioritize genes and RNA isoforms. Functional annotation will further characterize credible variants and candidate regulatory mechanisms. \[7–12\] These analyses use association summaries and LD matrices shared by sites, together with published GWAS results. They do not require sites to release participant-level childhood outcomes or other participant-level clinical data to MDACC. More advanced methods, including multivariate isoform-level TWAS, will be added after we confirm that they work with summary statistics from separate cohorts. 2.3 Test whether pregnancy conditions modify genetic effects Genotype-by-exposure (GxE) analysis will test whether the association between fetal genotype and placental RNA phenotypes changes with gestational exposures. The initial local workflow includes genotype-by-gestational-age interaction scans and, where sufficiently measured and permitted, interactions with pre-pregnancy BMI, gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), and oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) glucose. Exposure variables remain at the cohort site; only interaction statistics and aggregate exposure descriptors are requested. \[13\] In the first release, sites will run interaction tests separately for each eligible ancestry group. MDACC will combine results from cohorts with comparable exposures and models. Planned extensions will examine more extensive interaction statistics, colocalization of exposure-modified signals with GWAS loci, and whether exposure-dependent regulatory annotations are enriched for childhood metabolic trait heritability. 2.4 Interpret the findings We plan to report placental xQTL associations across cohorts and ancestry groups, likely causal variants, comparisons across types of RNA measurements, genes and isoforms prioritized at GWAS loci, and genetic effects that vary with gestational exposures. Public results will report combined findings. Cohort-specific results will be shared only as agreed with each participating cohort. 3. Data and computing needed at each cohort The pipeline is intended for cohorts with fetal genotype data (SNP arrays, whole-exome sequencing, or whole-genome sequencing where suitable for downstream imputation and QC) and placental bulk RNA-seq. Broad transcript coverage, such as total RNA-seq, is important for isoform, splicing, transcript-end, and RNA-editing analyses; 3′-capture assays may not support the complete modality set. Data availability and sequencing design will be reviewed with each site before analysis. Each site runs the analyses on its own research computing system using a supplied, self-contained software container that includes the reference data and runs without internet access, which keeps software and reference versions consistent across sites. After approval, MDACC also supplies by email a small restricted file containing the shared splicing reference clusters and the list of MDACC xQTL signals that every site tests for cell-type and exposure interactions. It uses the site’s fetal genotypes, RNA sequencing data, and a limited sample metadata table. Required local metadata are an RNA-seq identifier, genotype identifier, fetal sex, and gestational age at delivery. Optional local metadata include pre-pregnancy BMI, GDM, OGTT glucose, maternal age, parity, and smoking; interaction modules are enabled only when relevant variables and sufficient samples are available. Genotype imputation is required and must be performed through the TOPMed Imputation Server. Each participating site is responsible for uploading quality-controlled genotype files directly to the TOPMed Imputation Server in accordance with its terms of use and the site’s data-governance requirements. \[15\] 6. Files requested from each cohort Each site prepares summary files separately for each eligible ancestry group. Variants are identified by GRCh38 chromosome, position, and reference and alternate alleles. RNA features use the common annotation IDs and coordinates. The files contain no sample identifiers or participant-level records. The main requested results are variant-by-feature effect estimates (betas), standard errors (SEs), p-values, minor-allele frequencies (MAFs), minor-allele counts (MACs), sample sizes, and LD matrices. Data sharing and safeguards Files sent to MDACC exclude individual genotypes or sequencing reads (FASTQ/BAM), participant identifiers, per-sample molecular or clinical data, exposure values, latent factors, or cell-type proportions. Summary results are prepared separately for ancestry groups with at least 50 analyzed samples. MDACC will store approved shared files on access-controlled research computing infrastructure and use them for the collaborative placental xQTL analyses described here. Per-cohort files will not be redistributed or publicly released without the contributing cohort’s agreement. Publicly released findings will combine results across cohorts. Authorship, acknowledgement, access, and any additional uses should be established with collaborators in advance. 8. Setup This page takes a site from nothing to a working installation: get the image, check it, export the launcher, and confirm that the cluster can run the pipeline. It takes about 30 minutes plus the image download. Restricted file: request it before you start. Site runs need xqtl-restricted-<version>.tar.gz, a small file holding the shared (frozen) splicing clusters and the MDACC signal list. It is not in the image or on any public server. MDACC sends it by email to sites with an approved data-sharing agreement. If you have not received it, request it from Sean T. Bresnahan (stbresnahan@mdanderson.org), stating: your cohort name, the pipeline version you will run (for example 1.0.0), and the approved agreement (title or reference number). Keep the file inside your secure environment and set its path as restricted: in cohort.yml. The smoke test (step 5) reports whether it is present and intact. What you need Requirement Details Linux, x86-64 Login/head node plus compute nodes (or a single large workstation) Apptainer ≥ 1.0 or Singularity ≥ 3.8 On every node that runs tasks. Check with apptainer --version or singularity --version A batch scheduler (optional) LSF, SLURM, PBS Pro/Torque or SGE. See HPC configuration Shared filesystem Visible from the head node and all compute nodes, for the work directory and results Disk The image file (its size is listed on the release page and the Zenodo record), plus work space for your cohort (see HPC configuration) Internet Only to download the image once. Nothing at run time Nothing else is installed on the host: no conda, Java, Nextflow, R or Python. All of them come from the image. 1. Get the image The image is one file, xqtl-federated_<version>.sif, available from two places that hold the same bytes. From the GitHub container registry (needs outbound HTTPS to ghcr.io from the machine you download on): apptainer pull xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif oras://ghcr.io/sbresnahan/xqtl-federated-sif:1.0.0 # Singularity: singularity pull xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif oras://ghcr.io/sbresnahan/xqtl-federated-sif:1.0.0 From Zenodo (a plain HTTPS download; works through most proxies and can be done on a laptop and copied over): download xqtl-federated_<version>.sif and xqtl-federated_<version>.sif.sha256 from the Zenodo record linked on the GitHub release page. Verify the download. The checksum file is attached to the GitHub release and to the Zenodo record: sha256sum -c xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif.sha256 # must print: xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif: OK Put the .sif on the shared filesystem, for example next to where you will keep the launcher. One copy serves every run; compute nodes read it directly, so no image cache is needed. A Docker image of the same build (ghcr.io/sbresnahan/placenta-xqtl-federated:<version>) exists for workstations and continuous integration. Most clusters do not allow Docker; use the .sif. 2. Check the image apptainer run xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif help # commands available in the image apptainer run xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif versions # software versions (TSV) apptainer run xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif refs-check # verify the embedded reference data (sha256; ~1 min) refs-check compares every embedded reference file with the checksums recorded for this release and ends with OK <n> reference files verified. A failure means the image file is damaged; download it again. 3. Export the launcher (bootstrap) Nextflow’s head job runs on the host, outside the container, so it can submit jobs to your scheduler. bootstrap copies what the head job needs out of the image into a directory you choose: apptainer run xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif bootstrap ./xqtl Written Contents xqtl/run_xqtl.sh The launcher you run from now on xqtl/pipeline/ Pipeline code (identical to the copy in the image) xqtl/jre/ Java 17 runtime for the head job xqtl/nextflow/ Nextflow launcher (self-contained build) and its home directory xqtl/docs/ This documentation for offline reading: open xqtl/docs/index.html xqtl/VERSIONS.tsv, xqtl/XQTL_VERSION, xqtl/refs_MANIFEST.tsv Software versions, pipeline version, reference checksums The reference data stay inside the image; tasks read them at /opt/xqtl/refs. Notes: The destination must be on a filesystem visible inside the container. Apptainer binds $HOME and the current directory by default; for other locations add -B /path (for example apptainer run -B /scratch xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif bootstrap /scratch/xqtl). bootstrap records the path of the .sif in run_xqtl.sh. If you move the image later, set XQTL_SIF=/new/path/xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif before running, or bootstrap again. Use one directory per pipeline version. bootstrap refuses to write into a directory that already holds an installation; --force replaces the exported files and leaves your own files, work directories and results untouched. If bootstrap says it cannot tell where the .sif is (this happens with some older Singularity versions), add --sif /full/path/xqtl-federated_1.0.0.sif. 4. What run_xqtl.sh does run_xqtl.sh runs nextflow run xqtl/pipeline/main.nf --sif <image> <your arguments> with: Setting Value Why JAVA_HOME xqtl/jre No Java needed on the host NXF_HOME xqtl/nextflow/home Nextflow keeps its files inside the installation, not in $HOME/.nextflow NXF_OFFLINE true Nextflow never tries to reach the internet (on seadragon each attempt cost about 130 s) NXF_OPTS -Xms1g -Xmx4g unless you set it Head-job memory; see HPC configuration XQTL_SIF the .sif path Every task runs in this image Any NXF_VER, NXF_JAVA_HOME or JAVA_CMD in your environment is ignored, so a Nextflow or Java installation already on the host cannot interfere. Run it from the directory where you want the work directory and results, usually on scratch: cd /scratch/$USER/xqtl_run /path/to/xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile <site profile> -params-file cohort.yml --mode <mode> Long runs should be launched as a batch job or inside tmux/screen; see Running the head inside a batch job and the templates in pipeline/assets/head_job/. 5. Check that your cluster works (smoke test) /path/to/xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile seadragon,smoke --restricted /secure/path/xqtl-restricted-1.tar.gz # other sites: -profile slurm,apptainer,smoke -c conf/sites/<yoursite>.config ... The smoke test takes about 10 minutes and runs 12 checks (container start-up, tools, references, restricted file, job fan-out and arrays, memory enforcement, filesystem binds, a small tensorQTL run). It writes xqtl_smoke/smoke/smoke_summary.tsv ending in VERDICT GO or VERDICT NO-GO. HPC configuration explains each check and what to do about a FAIL or WARN. Send MDACC the summary file if you would like a second opinion; it holds no data. 6. Build the alignment indices (once per site) STAR, Salmon and IRFinder-S indices are too large to ship in the image, so each site builds them once from the references inside it: /path/to/xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile <site profile> -params-file cohort.yml --mode prepare_references The indices are written to site_refs: in cohort.yml and reused by every later run. This mode becomes available with the phenotyping release (see the changelog). Upgrading to a new pipeline version Download and verify the new .sif (step 1). Bootstrap it into a new directory, for example ./xqtl-1.1.0. Check the changelog: a new major version changes the export format or the restricted-file version, and MDACC will send a new restricted file. Re-run the smoke test. Site indices from prepare_references are reused unless the changelog says otherwise. Keep the old directory until the new version has run; results record the version that produced them. Offline documentation Every image carries this documentation. After bootstrap, open xqtl/docs/index.html in a browser (copy the folder to a laptop if the cluster has no browser). apptainer run <sif> docs prints its location inside the image. The online copy is at https://sbresnahan.github.io/placenta-xqtl-federated/.

HPC configuration guide This guide explains how the pipeline requests compute resources and how to adapt it to your cluster. Most sites only need to choose a profile, copy one site template and set five or six values. Validate every new configuration with the smoke test (see Validating a new site) before running real data. The pipeline runs in two parts: The head is a small Java process (Nextflow) that runs on a login node, a workflow node or inside a batch job. It submits every task to the scheduler and tracks it. It needs about 1 CPU and 2–4 GB of memory for the whole run, which can take several days. Tasks are batch jobs. Each task runs inside the same pipeline image (a .sif file, run with Apptainer or Singularity) on a compute node. Neither part needs internet access. The image contains all software and public reference data, and run_xqtl.sh (written by the image’s bootstrap command; see Setup) starts Nextflow in offline mode. Configuration layers Resource settings are layered so that the pipeline code never contains anything site-specific: Layer File What it sets Who edits it 1. Process labels modules/, workflows/ Each process declares a resource class (label 'process_medium'), never a queue, account or path Pipeline developers 2. Resource classes conf/base.config CPUs, memory and walltime for each class; retry policy; queue selection rule; caps Rarely changed 3. Executor profile conf/executors/<scheduler>.config Scheduler type, job submission rate, polling Rarely changed 4. Container profile conf/containers/<engine>.config Apptainer, Singularity or Docker; bind paths Rarely changed 5. Site profile conf/sites/<site>.config Queues, account codes, GPU syntax, bind paths, node limits Each site 6. Command line --max_memory 64.GB etc. Overrides any parameter for one run Each run Later layers override earlier ones. Profiles are combined with commas, for example -profile slurm,apptainer, and a site file is added with -c conf/sites/<site>.config. Seadragon has a built-in profile that bundles layers 3–5: -profile seadragon. To see the configuration that a combination resolves to, without running anything: nextflow config -profile slurm,apptainer -c conf/sites/mysite.config . Resource classes Defined in conf/base.config. Memory and time are multiplied by the attempt number, so a task that is killed for exceeding its memory or walltime is resubmitted with twice (then three times) as much. Process names are listed in the execution report (<outdir>/pipeline_info/report_*.html). Caps (--max_cpus, --max_memory, --max_time) Every request is capped at --max_cpus, --max_memory and --max_time (Nextflow process.resourceLimits). Set these to the largest node and longest queue you may use; a request above the cap is lowered to the cap instead of being rejected by the scheduler. Defaults are 16 CPUs, 128 GB and 120 h. Check node sizes with bhosts -l / lshosts (LSF), sinfo -o "%n %c %m" (SLURM), pbsnodes -a (PBS) or qhost (SGE). Executors Scheduler Profile Notes IBM Spectrum LSF lsf Memory is per job (perJobMemLimit); see Memory SLURM slurm --mem per job by default; --mem-per-cpu option in the template PBS Pro / OpenPBS pbspro select=1:ncpus=N:mem=M syntax Torque / PBS pbs nodes=1:ppn=N,mem=M syntax SGE / UGE / Son of Grid Engine sge Uses parallel environment smp; change it if your site uses another name No scheduler (one large node) local All tasks run on the head’s node; capped by --max_cpus / --max_memory Site templates with every value marked EDIT are in conf/sites/: TEMPLATE_slurm.config TEMPLATE_lsf.config TEMPLATE_pbspro.config (also works for Torque with -profile pbs) TEMPLATE_sge.config Copy one to conf/sites/<yoursite>.config, edit it and run with: ./run_xqtl.sh -profile slurm,apptainer -c conf/sites/<yoursite>.config -params-file cohort.yml --mode smoke Single node (-profile local) On a workstation or one large allocated node, -profile local,apptainer runs every task on that machine, never using more than --max_cpus and --max_memory at once. A full cohort needs many CPU-days (see Tuning); this mode suits small cohorts, the smoke test and re-running the export. Queues and partitions Many schedulers reject or misroute jobs whose walltime does not fit the queue. The pipeline chooses a queue for each task from its walltime with --queue_rules: --queue_rules 'short:3h,medium:23h59m,long:120h' Rules are read left to right; the first queue whose limit is at least the task’s walltime is used, and the last queue takes anything longer. Because walltime grows with each retry, a retried task can move to a longer queue automatically. List queues in increasing walltime order. --queue NAME sends every task to one queue and ignores the rules. With neither set, no queue is requested and the scheduler’s default is used. --gpu_queue is used only for GPU tasks with --use_gpu. Find your limits with bqueues -l (LSF), scontrol show partition (SLURM), qstat -Qf (PBS) or qconf -sq <queue> (SGE). Memory The scheduler must receive the same memory number that the task will use, and in the units it expects. Getting this wrong is the most common cause of jobs being killed or never starting. LSF perJobMemLimit = true (the default here, --lsf_per_job_mem true) tells Nextflow that memory limits apply to the whole job. Without it, Nextflow divides the request by the number of CPUs, and multi-core tasks are killed far below their request on clusters configured per job. Nextflow reads LSF_UNIT_FOR_LIMITS from $LSF_ENVDIR/lsf.conf to choose the unit for -M and rusage[mem=...]. The head must therefore run in a shell where the LSF environment is loaded (LSF_ENVDIR set). Check one submitted script (.command.run in any task directory) and confirm that the #BSUB -M value is in the unit your site expects. If LSB_MEMLIMIT_ENFORCE=y (as on seadragon), a task that exceeds its request is killed with exit status 130 and retried with more memory. To check how your site is configured: grep -E 'LSF_UNIT_FOR_LIMITS|LSB_MEMLIMIT_ENFORCE|LSB_RESOURCE_ENFORCE|LSB_JOB_MEMLIMIT' $LSF_ENVDIR/lsf.conf SLURM By default the pipeline requests memory per job (--mem). This is correct on almost all SLURM sites. Some sites require --mem-per-cpu. The SLURM template contains a commented clusterOptions line that converts the request; enable it if jobs are rejected with a memory-specification error. Sites that set DefMemPerCPU without enforcing --mem can still kill jobs through cgroups; the smoke test (S10) shows whether memory is enforced. PBS and SGE PBS Pro: memory goes into the select statement (mem=), per job. Torque: -l mem= per job; some Torque sites need pmem (per process) instead. Add it with --cluster_options. SGE: memory is requested with -l h_vmem (per slot on many sites). If your site expects per-slot values, divide the request in your site file: process.clusterOptions = { "-l h_vmem=${(task.memory.toMega() / task.cpus) as int}M" } Retries after memory or time kills conf/base.config retries a task up to 3 times when it exits with a status that schedulers use for resource kills: 104, 130, 134, 137, 139, 140, 143, 247 or 271. Other failures stop the run after running tasks finish (errorStrategy 'finish'), so you can fix the problem and continue with -resume. If a task fails with a resource error on all attempts, raise its class or the cap in your site file rather than editing the pipeline. CPUs and threads Each tool receives the number of CPUs from task.cpus explicitly (for example STAR --runThreadN ${task.cpus}, salmon -p, plink2 --threads, torch.set_num_threads). Tools therefore never use more cores than requested, even on schedulers that do not confine CPUs. The container receives the scheduler’s job variables (LSB_*, SLURM_*, PBS_*, JOB_ID, SGE_TASK_ID, NSLOTS) through the engine’s environment whitelist. Every multi-threaded process also sets OMP_NUM_THREADS, MKL_NUM_THREADS and OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS to task.cpus, which keeps R and numpy linear algebra within the request. On LSF sites with LSB_RESOURCE_ENFORCE="cpu" (seadragon), a task only sees the cores it requested; the smoke test reports this (S06 shows nproc equal to the request). Job arrays, queue size and submission rate Job arrays. Processes with many short identical tasks (per-chromosome or per-chunk steps, label process_array) are submitted as job arrays of up to --job_array_size tasks (default 50). This reduces scheduler load and queue wait. Arrays work with LSF, SLURM, PBS Pro and SGE; the local executor ignores them. --job_array_size 0 turns arrays off. --queue_size (default 100; seadragon 200) is the maximum number of jobs Nextflow keeps queued or running at once. Lower it if your site limits jobs per user. --submit_rate_limit (default '10 sec', meaning 10 submissions per second) throttles submission. Use '1 sec' or '30 min'-style values only if the scheduler administrators ask. Polling: status is checked every 30 s and the queue every 2 min, which is gentle on the scheduler. GPUs GPUs are optional. All tensorQTL steps run on CPU by default, which takes longer but needs nothing special. To use GPUs: Use the CUDA image (xqtl-federated_<version>-cuda.sif) through --sif. Add --use_gpu true. Set the GPU queue and request syntax in your site file: Scheduler gpu_cluster_options example LSF -gpu num=1 (seadragon) or -gpu "num=1:mode=shared" SLURM --gres=gpu:1 or --gpus=1 PBS Pro -l select=1:ngpus=1 SGE -l gpu=1 With --use_gpu, tasks labelled process_gpu_capable go to --gpu_queue, request 4 CPUs plus the GPU flags, and Apptainer/Singularity are started with --nv so the container can see the NVIDIA driver. Without it, the same tasks run on CPU with 8 CPUs. Results are numerically equivalent within floating-point tolerance. The smoke test checks GPU tensorQTL only when --use_gpu true is given. Container runtime Apptainer or Singularity Apptainer ≥ 1.0 is recommended (-profile <scheduler>,apptainer). On sites where Apptainer is installed under the name singularity, or where only SingularityCE ≥ 3.8 is available, use -profile <scheduler>,singularity. Seadragon is in this group (Apptainer 1.5 invoked as singularity). Docker is used only for CI (-profile test,docker). The image is a local file. run_xqtl.sh passes its path as --sif, so nothing is pulled at run time and no image cache is needed (NXF_APPTAINER_CACHEDIR and NXF_SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR are unused). Bind paths Inside the container, only paths that are bound are visible. autoMounts binds the work directory and the paths of input files automatically, but data reached through symlinks or listed inside a samplesheet often live on other filesystems. List every filesystem that holds FASTQs, genotypes, the restricted file, the work directory and outputs: --bind_paths '/scratch,/project,/data' The smoke test checks a path you choose with --bind_test_path /project/somefile.txt (S09). Work directory, temporary space and cleanup Work directory (-w). Every task runs in its own subdirectory of the work directory. Put it on a large shared filesystem visible to all compute nodes, ideally scratch: -w /scratch/$USER/xqtl_work. A full cohort produces about 2 TB of transient alignment files at peak. Temporary files. Tasks write temporary files inside their work directory, not to /tmp, because /tmp on compute nodes is often small. To use fast node-local disk instead, set process.scratch = '/local/scratch' (or '$TMPDIR') in your site file; Nextflow then runs each task in that directory and copies outputs back. Apptainer build/temp directories are not used at run time, since nothing is built or pulled. Cleanup. Keep the work directory until the run has finished and the export has been reviewed, because -resume needs it. Then delete it, or run nextflow clean -f -before <last run name> from the launch directory. Intermediate BAMs are deleted by the pipeline once their counts are written. Running offline Compute nodes at most sites have no internet access, and the pipeline never needs it: NXF_OFFLINE=true is set by run_xqtl.sh. Without it, Nextflow tries to contact www.nextflow.io at every launch; on seadragon that added about 130 s per launch before timing out. No plugins. The pipeline uses no Nextflow plugins, so nothing is downloaded at launch. Input validation is done by a Python step inside the image (bin/xqtl_validate.py). The launcher is exported from the image. apptainer run <sif> bootstrap ./xqtl copies the pipeline code, a Java runtime and the Nextflow launcher out of the image, and writes run_xqtl.sh with JAVA_HOME, NXF_HOME and the image path set. The host needs only Apptainer or Singularity and a scheduler. References are inside the image. Processes read the public references from /opt/xqtl/refs inside the container. Indices that must be built for your read length are written once by --mode prepare_references to --site_refs. Running the head inside a batch job Running Nextflow on a login node is fine for short runs, but many sites kill long login-node processes. For full runs, submit the head as an ordinary batch job; it then submits tasks as further jobs. Phase 0 confirmed this works on seadragon (head job on the medium queue). Templates are in assets/head_job/ (lsf.sh, slurm.sh, pbs.sh, sge.sh). The essential settings are: Setting Value Why CPUs 1–2 The head does little computation Memory 4–8 GB Java heap plus headroom NXF_OPTS -Xms1g -Xmx4g Keeps the JVM within the job’s memory limit Walltime Longest queue (e.g. 120 h) The head must outlive all tasks; resume if it is killed Queue One that allows jobs to submit jobs Some sites forbid submission from compute nodes; ask your administrators Example for LSF: #BSUB -J xqtl_head #BSUB -q long #BSUB -W 120:00 #BSUB -n 1 #BSUB -M 8 #BSUB -R "rusage[mem=8]" #BSUB -o xqtl_head.%J.out export NXF_OPTS="-Xms1g -Xmx4g" cd "$LS_SUBCWD" ./xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile seadragon -params-file cohort.yml --mode site -resume If the head job is killed, resubmit it with -resume: finished tasks are reused, and jobs that were still running are resubmitted. Site-specific settings Account, project and QOS codes Put flags required on every job in --cluster_options, usually in your site file: Scheduler Example LSF -P myproject or -G mygroup SLURM --account=myproj --qos=normal PBS -A myproject SGE -P myproject GPU tasks receive both cluster_options and gpu_cluster_options. Module systems Nothing needs to be loaded inside tasks, because all software is in the image. On the head node, Apptainer or Singularity must be on PATH for the head and for the batch jobs. If your site provides it as a module, add module load apptainer to your shell profile or to the head job script, and add process.beforeScript = 'module load apptainer' to your site file if compute nodes do not inherit it. Validating a new site Before running real data, run the smoke test with exactly the profile you will use for real runs: ./xqtl/run_xqtl.sh -profile seadragon,smoke --bind_test_path /rsrch5/home/$USER/somefile.txt \ --restricted /path/to/xqtl-restricted-1.tar.gz For other sites: -profile slurm,apptainer,smoke -c conf/sites/mysite.config. Then run the same command again with -resume; every task should be reported as cached. The test takes 5–15 minutes, depending on queue wait, and uses only synthetic data generated inside the tasks. Results are written to xqtl_smoke/smoke/smoke_summary.tsv, ending with VERDICT GO or NO-GO: Test What it checks If it fails S01 container R The image starts on compute nodes; R 4.3.1 runs Engine not on PATH on compute nodes; wrong --sif path; image not readable from nodes S02 embedded tools Every tool in the image reports a version (tool_versions.tsv) Wrong or damaged image; re-verify the sha256 S03 embedded references Reference files match the image manifest Wrong image or --refs_dir S04 restricted file The restricted file opens, has the expected version and checksums WARN if not given; FAIL if damaged or the wrong version. Request it by email (see Setup) S05 plink2 Genotype tooling runs Image problem S06 resources 4 CPUs and 8 GB are granted; a 4 GB allocation succeeds; whether CPUs are confined (scheduler view in sched_view.txt) Memory units or per-job/per-slot setting wrong (see Memory) S07 fan-out 5 independent jobs run, usually on several nodes Queue or account settings S08 job array A 5-task job array runs Arrays disabled at your site: set --job_array_size 0 S09 bind read A file on your project filesystem is visible in the container Add the filesystem to --bind_paths S10 memory enforcement and retry A task that exceeds its 2 GB request is killed and retried with 4 GB WARN means memory is not enforced; set --max_memory conservatively S11 tensorQTL CPU (or GPU with --use_gpu) cis-mapping recovers a planted signal Image or GPU driver problem S12 Storey q-value The R qvalue bridge runs on tensorQTL output Image problem WARN and SKIP lines do not block a GO, but they tell you which defaults to adjust. Send the summary file to MDACC with your first export. Worked example: seadragon (MD Anderson) Seadragon runs IBM LSF with Apptainer 1.5.1, invoked as singularity. The built-in profile conf/sites/seadragon.config encodes the Phase 0 results (appendix Seadragon validation): includeConfig '../executors/lsf.config' includeConfig '../containers/singularity.config' params { queue_rules = 'short:3h,medium:23h59m,long:120h' gpu_queue = 'gpu' gpu_cluster_options = '-gpu num=1' bind_paths = '/rsrch5,/rsrch9' max_cpus = 16 max_memory = '120.GB' max_time = '120.h' queue_size = 200 } executor { perJobMemLimit = true } Why each value: Queues. Seadragon’s submission filter (esub) rejects walltimes outside each queue’s range: short ≤ 3 h, medium more than 3 h and under 24 h, long 24–120 h. The rule medium:23h59m keeps 24-hour tasks out of medium. Memory. LSF_UNIT_FOR_LIMITS=GB and LSB_MEMLIMIT_ENFORCE=y: memory is per job, in GB, and enforced. Phase 0 saw the over-limit task killed with exit 130 and retried successfully with 4 GB. CPUs. LSB_RESOURCE_ENFORCE="cpu gpu" confines each job to its requested cores (Phase 0: nproc=4 for a 4-core request). Bind paths. Project data live on /rsrch5 and /rsrch9. Network. Compute nodes have no internet. Of the container registries, ghcr.io and quay.io were reachable from login nodes at about 0.6 MB/s; Docker Hub, gcr.io and Amazon ECR were blocked or unreliable. Download the SIF once (about 3–4 h at that speed) or copy it by Globus. Building images. apptainer build --fakeroot with package installation fails on seadragon (apt exit 100). Never build images there; use the published SIF. Head. Both a login-node head and a head inside an LSF job (medium queue, 1 core, 4 GB) passed Phase 0. Export specification This page describes the folder a site shares with MDACC after --mode site (or --mode export). It is written to <outdir>/export/ and holds only summary statistics. Everything else under <outdir>/ stays at the site, including site/, pipeline_info/ and the work directory. Files A–F, I and J are produced from pipeline version 1.0.0 onwards. Files G (cell-type interaction, G×C) and H (exposure interaction, GxE) are added by later milestones. The export format is versioned with the pipeline (see the changelog). Layout export/<cohort_id>/ MANIFEST.tsv J every file: path, sha256, bytes, rows, class, versions DATA_DICTIONARY.md J column definitions <cohort_id>_cohort_I_strata.tsv I ancestry strata: n individuals, n RNA-seq samples, status <ANC>/ one folder per mapped ancestry stratum (n >= ancestry.min_n) A_nominal/<cohort>_<ANC>_A_nominal_<modality>_<chrom>.parquet B_mapping/<cohort>_<ANC>_B_permutation_<arm>.parquet B_mapping/<cohort>_<ANC>_B_independent_<arm>.parquet C_ld/<cohort>_<ANC>_C_ld_<chrom>_<start>_<end>.npz (+ .variants.tsv.gz, C_ld.windows.tsv) <cohort>_<ANC>_D_variant_qc.parquet <cohort>_<ANC>_E_features.parquet <cohort>_<ANC>_F_model_settings.json <cohort>_<ANC>_I_summary.parquet With export.format: tsv.gz, tables are written as gzipped TSV instead of Parquet. Variant IDs are GRCh38 chr:pos:ref:alt. Effects are per copy of the ALT allele, in normalized phenotype units. Arms. A modality with feature groups (for example splicing, where IDs are GENE__feature) is mapped twice: grouped, one test per gene, arm <modality>; ungrouped, one test per feature, arm <modality>_ungrouped. Modalities without groups have one arm. The combined arm maps all modalities of a gene together as one group (PANTRY-style). File classes Class Content Key columns A all cis variant–phenotype pairs within mapping.cis_window (ungrouped, per modality and chromosome) phenotype_id, variant_id, chrom, pos, ref, alt, effect_allele, other_allele, tss_distance, eaf, maf, ma_count, n, beta, se, pval B tensorQTL map_cis lead per phenotype or group, with beta-approximated permutation p-values and q-values; conditionally independent signals from map_independent arm, phenotype_id, variant_id, slope, slope_se, pval_nominal, pval_beta, qval, qvalue_method, (group_id, group_size), rank C in-sample LD: signed r stored as float16, for variants with MAF ≥ ld.maf_min and imputation R² ≥ ld.rsq_min, in ld.window_mb windows with a ld.step_mb step. Each .npz holds exactly one square matrix R; the row order is in the matching .variants.tsv.gz R; variant_id, chrom, pos, ref, alt, eaf D per-variant QC in the stratum variant_id, eaf, maf, n, hwe_p, rsq, typed E phenotype features: coordinates (gene TSS), group, detection fraction, filter status modality, phenotype_id, chr, start, end, detection_fraction, status, group_id F model settings: normalization, HCP grid with eGene counts, selected k, covariate names (no values), permutations, window, MAF threshold, seed JSON I aggregate counts (genotype QC steps, normalization), and 5/25/50/75/95 % quantiles, mean and SD of sequencing metrics and cell-type proportions (computed only when n ≥ 10) table, item, statistic, value J manifest with sha256 and the image sha256, restricted-file version and pipeline version; data dictionary What is never exported Sample, RNA-seq or genotype identifiers. Per-sample values of any kind: genotypes, dosages, phenotypes, covariates, genotype or HCP PCs, ancestry assignments, outlier lists. Minimum or maximum values. The site keeps these under <outdir>/site/ for its own records. Leak scan The leak scan runs at the end of every export and cannot be disabled. It collects every identifier from: the metadata columns rnaseq_id and genotype_id; the samplesheet sample_id column; all sample IDs in the imputed VCFs. It then checks every exported file. The export fails if any of the following is found: an identifier in a file name, a column name or any text value. Identifiers are matched as whole tokens, so S001 matches reads_S001 but not S0010. Purely numeric or very short IDs are matched only as a complete value. Variant IDs are exempt; an .npz file that holds anything other than one square matrix R; a file type other than Parquet, TSV, gzipped TSV, NPZ, JSON or Markdown. When the scan fails, the export folder is deleted and the run stops. The findings are written to leak_report.tsv in the task work directory; it is local only and must not be shared. Fix the cause, then rebuild the export with --mode export. Rebuilding the export --mode export rebuilds export/ from a finished site run without recomputing anything, for example after changing export.format or export.round_digits. It reads: <outdir>/site/ancestry/cohort_strata.tsv; the per-stratum folders <outdir>/site/<ANC>/; <outdir>/site/genotype_qc/cohort.vcf_samples.txt; <outdir>/site/restricted_version.txt. Any previous export/ folder is removed first. Phenotype inputs (phenotypes_dir) --mode site normally builds phenotypes from FASTQs. If phenotypes_dir is set, it maps ready inputs instead, and site_refs is not required. The directory must contain: File Content <modality>.bed.gz one per modality in mapping.modalities. BED columns #chr start end phenotype_id, then one column per RNA-seq sample. Coordinates are the gene TSS (start = TSS - 1, end = TSS), so all features of a gene share one cis window. Grouped modalities use GENE__feature IDs expression.counts.bed.gz raw gene counts in the same layout (used for TMM-VST) qc_metrics.tsv sample column + sequencing QC metrics (used for HCP and file I) cell_proportions.tsv sample column + estimated cell-type proportions (optional) Site-side processing behind the export Step Method (atlas-compatible) Genotype QC TOPMed R² ≥ qc.rsq_min, biallelic. Dosages are kept and hard calls are the nearest genotype. Per-stratum MAF, MAC, HWE and missingness filters, then PC outliers (6 SD on PC1–5) are removed Ancestry PC-AiR on KING-robust kinship against the 1000 Genomes panel. Each sample gets the nearest superpopulation centroid on PCs 1–10. Samples are “unassigned” if the QDA posterior for that label is below ancestry.assign_prob_min. Strata below ancestry.min_n are counted but not mapped Normalization Expression: TMM-VST, then removal of connectivity outliers (bicor z < −3). Other modalities: quantile normalization + inverse normal transform. Technical replicates are averaged after normalization Covariates Sex, genotype PCs 1–5, cell-type proportions (dominant type dropped, gxc.exclude_cell_types removed, arcsinh) and HCP factors. Pruned at |r| > 0.9, keeping the higher-priority covariate k selection The HCP grid is mapping.hcp_grid, or by default 0–60 by 10 (n < 350) or 0–100 by 10. Values of k that leave fewer than 20 residual degrees of freedom are skipped. k* gives the most eGenes on mapping.eval_chrom, or genome-wide if that chromosome has fewer than mapping.eval_min_phenotypes phenotypes. Ties go to the smaller k. The grouped and ungrouped arms share k* Mapping tensorQTL map_cis (mapping.nperm permutations, Storey q-values with a BH fallback recorded in qvalue_method), map_independent in chunks of mapping.independent_chunk_size, and map_nominal

Reference data and software provenance Everything a site run reads, apart from the cohort’s own data and the restricted file, is inside the image. This page records where each embedded file comes from, how it is checked, and how MDACC builds and releases it. Embedded reference data The image holds the public references at /opt/xqtl/refs. The build downloads each file, verifies it against a sha256 pinned in assets/refs_sources.tsv, processes it with the image’s own tools, and writes a checksum list, /opt/xqtl/refs/MANIFEST.tsv. That list must equal assets/refs_manifest.tsv for a release build to succeed. apptainer run <sif> refs-check repeats the comparison at any time, and bootstrap exports the list as refs_MANIFEST.tsv. its record number is pinned on the # ZENODO_RECORD= line of assets/refs_sources.tsv. Primary-source files (genome, chain) are downloaded from their original servers and pinned by sha256; their published MD5s were checked when they were pinned (genome a08035b6a6e31780e96a34008ff21bd6, chain 35887f73fe5e2231656504d1f6430900). Genome The atlas aligned to a cleaned copy of the GRCh38 no-alt analysis set (..._cleaned_ready_for_salmon.fasta). The image ships the original NCBI file. During the build, fetch_references.sh compares the contig names, lengths and sequence MD5s of the shipped genome with atlas_genome_contigs.tsv from the MDACC record and prints either genome: identical to the atlas genome or the contigs that differ. Any difference is reviewed before a release and recorded in the changelog. Ancestry PCA panel (deviation from the atlas) The atlas pruned each cohort’s genotypes (MAF ≥ 0.05, missingness ≤ 0.05, --indep-pairwise 1000 100 0.1) and intersected them with the full 1000 Genomes high-coverage panel (chr:pos:ref:alt IDs). Shipping the full panel would add many gigabytes to the image, so the federated panel is pre-filtered: biallelic autosomal A/C/G/T SNPs of the 1000 Genomes samples with super-population labels, duplicate IDs removed, MAF ≥ 0.05 in 1000 Genomes, then --indep-pairwise 1000 100 0.2. Sites still prune their own genotypes at the atlas setting (1000 100 0.1) and intersect with this panel. The looser panel threshold keeps more candidate SNPs than the cohort-side prune, so the intersection should be close to what the atlas used. Ancestry assignments from this panel are to be compared with the atlas assignments before the first release. RNA-editing sites (REDIportal) The atlas used REDIportal sites to define the RNA-editing phenotype. REDIportal’s terms for redistributing the site list have not been confirmed, so this file is optional: it is left out of the MDACC record (INCLUDE_REDIPORTAL=no) until the terms are confirmed. Without it, the RNA-editing phenotype will take a site-supplied BED of editing sites (a parameter added with the phenotyping release). Built at each site STAR, Salmon and IRFinder-S indices are tens of gigabytes and depend on the aligner versions, so they are not shipped. --mode prepare_references builds them once per site from the genome and annotation above, into site_refs:. Not public: the restricted file xqtl-restricted-<version>.tar.gz holds the frozen leafCutter cluster set (atlas clusters merged across cohorts and ancestries, junction coordinates only) and the MDACC signal list (atlas lead and conditionally independent cis-signals at q ≤ 0.05 for nine modalities and both ancestry groups, as variant and phenotype IDs). It contains no per-sample data, but it is not published. MDACC sends it by email to approved sites; request it from Sean T. Bresnahan (stbresnahan@mdanderson.org), stating your cohort, the pipeline version and the approved agreement. The pipeline checks its version and internal checksums before use. Software All software versions are pinned (see containers/env/*.yml, containers/requirements-pip.txt, containers/install_r_extra.R, containers/build_irfinder.sh and the ARG lines of containers/Dockerfile). The exact resolved versions are in the image at /opt/xqtl/VERSIONS.tsv and /opt/xqtl/env_lock/, printed by apptainer run <sif> versions, exported by bootstrap, and attached to each GitHub release. Notes on how the image differs from a straight copy of the atlas environment: Two conda environments. Salmon 1.10.2 and the R/ICU stack need conflicting libraries, so the aligners (STAR, Salmon) live in a separate align environment. Both are on PATH; nothing changes for users. IRFinder-S is compiled from source (release v2.0.1, commit-verified) in a separate build stage. Java and Nextflow are a pinned Temurin 17 runtime and the self-contained Nextflow distribution, both checksum-verified at build time and exported to the host by bootstrap. GPU variant. -cuda images use PyTorch wheels built for CUDA 13.2 (cu132), the oldest CUDA build published for the pinned PyTorch release. GPU nodes need an NVIDIA driver that supports CUDA 13.2 (check the CUDA version shown by nvidia-smi). The CPU image runs everywhere and is the default. MDACC maintainer procedures Building the public reference record (once per reference release) On seadragon, after confirming the paths marked CHECK in scripts/packaging/seadragon.env: module load plink samtools scripts/make_public_reference_record.sh --env scripts/packaging/seadragon.env --out /rsrch5/.../xqtl_public_refs --dry-run # lists every input, or MISSING scripts/make_public_reference_record.sh --env scripts/packaging/seadragon.env --out /rsrch5/.../xqtl_public_refs Upload every file in the output directory to a new public Zenodo record (CC-BY-4.0 for the MDACC-derived files), publish it, then pin it and commit: scripts/pin_reference_record.py --record <record id> --files /rsrch5/.../xqtl_public_refs/files.tsv git commit -m "Pin public reference record <id>" assets/refs_sources.tsv Building the restricted file scripts/make_restricted_bundle.sh --env scripts/packaging/seadragon.env --out /rsrch5/.../restricted --dry-run scripts/make_restricted_bundle.sh --env scripts/packaging/seadragon.env --out /rsrch5/.../restricted This writes xqtl-restricted-<version>.tar.gz and its .sha256. The archive is byte-reproducible: rebuilding from the same inputs gives the same checksum. Send it by institutional secure email, or as an encrypted archive with the password sent separately, to approved sites only. Building an image containers/build_image.sh downloads and verifies the references, renders this documentation if needed, and runs docker buildx build with the right build contexts and arguments: containers/build_image.sh # development build (unpinned rows allowed) containers/build_image.sh --variant cuda # GPU variant containers/build_image.sh --release # every row pinned; references must equal assets/refs_manifest.tsv Releasing a version Pin the public reference record (above) and push to main. The image workflow builds ghcr.io/sbresnahan/placenta-xqtl-federated:dev and uploads refs_MANIFEST.tsv as an artifact. Commit that file as assets/refs_manifest.tsv (first release, or whenever a reference changes). Set manifest.version in nextflow.config, update the changelog, and push the tag v<version>. The workflow then builds the CPU and -cuda images in strict mode, pushes them, builds the .sif, pushes it to ghcr.io/sbresnahan/xqtl-federated-sif:<version> (pulled with apptainer pull oras://...), archives it on Zenodo, and attaches the .sif checksum, reference manifest and version list to the GitHub release. One-time repository settings: Secret ZENODO_TOKEN: a Zenodo personal access token with deposit:write and deposit:actions. Optional repository variables: ZENODO_CONCEPT_ID (an earlier deposition of the image record, so every release becomes a new version under one concept DOI) and ZENODO_PUBLISH=true (publish automatically; otherwise the deposition is left as a draft to review on zenodo.org). Package visibility: after the first push, set both GHCR packages (placenta-xqtl-federated and xqtl-federated-sif) to public under the repository’s Packages settings, so sites can pull without logging in. Documentation site: Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → bookdown / (root). The docs workflow renders the book and pushes it to that branch.

Seadragon validation (Phase 0) Before the pipeline was written, a stand-alone smoke kit checked that every scheduler and container behaviour the pipeline relies on works on MD Anderson’s seadragon cluster. It was run on 2026-10-29 in both supported head modes. Both runs gave GO. The kit’s checks are now built into the pipeline as --mode smoke (see Validating a new site); test identifiers below are those of the Phase 0 kit, with the pipeline equivalent in brackets. Findings carried into the pipeline Queues. The site’s submission filter enforces walltime ranges (short ≤ 3 h; medium more than 3 h and under 24 h; long 24–120 h). The seadragon profile therefore picks the queue from each task’s walltime (queue_rules). Memory. LSF_UNIT_FOR_LIMITS=GB and LSB_MEMLIMIT_ENFORCE=y: memory is requested per job and enforced, and over-limit jobs exit with status 130. Exit 130 is in the pipeline’s retry list. CPU confinement. LSB_RESOURCE_ENFORCE="cpu gpu". No internet on compute nodes. Nextflow spent about 130 s per launch waiting for a connection to www.nextflow.io. run_xqtl.sh sets NXF_OFFLINE=true, and the image contains everything needed at run time. Registries. From login nodes ghcr.io and quay.io worked at about 0.6 MB/s; Docker Hub, gcr.io and Amazon ECR were blocked or unreliable. The pipeline image is published on ghcr.io and Zenodo. No image builds on seadragon. apptainer build --fakeroot with apt failed (exit 100). Images are built by GitHub Actions only. ps inside the image. Nextflow’s task wrapper needs ps; the image includes procps. q-values without rpy2. The atlas file bridge (compute_qvalues.R) is used for Storey q-values.

Changelog All notable changes to this pipeline are recorded here. Versions follow semantic versioning: a change in the export format (files A–J) or in the restricted-file version is a major version change. 1.0.0-dev (unreleased) Added Repository skeleton: main.nf with run modes, nextflow.config, resource classes (conf/base.config), executor profiles for LSF, SLURM, PBS Pro, Torque, SGE and local runs, Apptainer/Singularity/Docker profiles, the built-in seadragon profile and site templates. --mode smoke: site validation (12 checks with a GO / NO-GO verdict), folded in from the Phase 0 seadragon kit. Input validation (bin/xqtl_validate.py) against assets/schema/cohort.schema.json, run at the start of every mode, with --validate_only. Restricted-file tooling (bin/xqtl_restricted.py): byte-reproducible archive, version and checksum verification. Embedded-reference manifest check (bin/xqtl_refs_check.py) and tool version report (bin/xqtl_tool_versions.sh). Software environment definition (containers/env/, containers/requirements-pip.txt, containers/install_r_extra.R, containers/build_irfinder.sh) and scripts/dev_env.sh for local development. Documentation: collaboration brief, HPC configuration guide, seadragon validation; bookdown site builder (book/) and GitHub Pages workflow (.github/workflows/docs.yml). Offline image recipe (containers/Dockerfile): software environments, IRFinder-S, public references, Java 17 runtime, Nextflow 26.10.4, pipeline code and the rendered documentation in one image; entry point with bootstrap, versions, refs-check and docs commands. bootstrap (containers/bootstrap.sh): exports the pipeline, Java runtime, Nextflow and documentation to the host and writes run_xqtl.sh (offline Nextflow with the image path, JAVA_HOME and NXF_HOME set). Public reference data: sources pinned by sha256 (assets/refs_sources.tsv), download and deterministic processing (scripts/fetch_references.sh), release checksum list (assets/refs_manifest.tsv). MDACC packaging: scripts/make_public_reference_record.sh (Zenodo reference record, including the pre-pruned 1000 Genomes PCA panel), scripts/pin_reference_record.py, scripts/make_restricted_bundle.sh (frozen splicing clusters merged across ancestries, MDACC signal list), settings in scripts/packaging/seadragon.env. Image build and release: containers/build_image.sh; workflows ci.yml (unit tests, profile resolution, nextflow lint, shellcheck, hadolint, actionlint, image self-checks) and image.yml (development image on main; on a version tag: CPU and CUDA images, .sif pushed to GHCR as an OCI artifact, Zenodo archive via scripts/zenodo_upload.sh, release assets). Documentation: setup guide and reference-data provenance page. --mode site (genotypes to export, with ready phenotype inputs from phenotypes_dir): post-imputation QC and merge (xqtl_geno_qc.sh, xqtl_geno_merge.sh); ancestry strata from PC-AiR against the 1000 Genomes panel, with QDA-posterior confidence (xqtl_ancestry.sh, xqtl_ancestry.R); per-stratum genotype QC and PCs (xqtl_stratum_geno.sh); normalization (xqtl_normalize.R), HCP factors (xqtl_hcp.R), covariates (xqtl_covariates.py) and k selection (xqtl_select_k.py); tensorQTL permutation, chunked conditionally independent and nominal passes (xqtl_tensorqtl.py, xqtl_merge_parquet.py); the combined-modality arm (xqtl_combine_modalities.py) and in-sample LD (xqtl_ld.py). Export files A–F, I and J with a mandatory leak scan (xqtl_export.py); --mode export rebuilds the export from a finished site run. Specification: docs/EXPORT_SPEC.md. Test fixture tests/fixtures/site/: 130 1000 Genomes samples (chr22) with synthetic phenotypes and planted cis effects (make_site_fixture.sh). tests/scripts/test_site.sh checks signal recovery, the AFR below-minimum stratum and the leak scan end to end, and runs in CI with the development image. Fixed Image build: containers/install_r_extra.R now runs with the environment’s bin on PATH so Rhcpp and colocboost find the conda C++ compiler; it also stops early if the bioconda GenomeInfoDbData post-link download failed. CI: base image pinned by digest directly in the FROM lines (hadolint DL3006); actions/checkout and actions/setup-java v5. Leak scan: text columns were skipped under pandas >= 3 (new str dtype), so sample IDs in string columns of parquet/TSV exports could pass; the scanner now checks every non-numeric, non-boolean, non-datetime column. CI unit tests: dependencies pinned to the image versions (tests/requirements-ci.txt), plus a second run with the latest pandas/pyarrow/numpy. image.yml: references are downloaded and cached in their own steps (cached even when the build fails), the book is rendered in its own step, and a failed docker build posts its last log lines as a public annotation and uploads build.log. Changed image.yml no longer runs on pushes or tags until M6 is complete; manual runs still work. conf/test.config uses the site fixture and re-applies resourceLimits (2 CPU, 6 GB), because base.config evaluates the limits before profiles set params.max_*. Not yet available prepare_references, imputation_prep, phenotyping_only and central modes stop with a message until their milestones are complete. --mode site currently needs phenotypes_dir (FASTQ phenotyping arrives with M4), and G×C/GxE (files G and H) arrive with M5.
